desc:
Swap exactly two elements of nums (two different positions) so that the resulting array is the lexicographically largest array that is still smaller than nums. Return it.

If no single swap can make the array lexicographically smaller, return nums unchanged. Values may repeat.

nums = [3, 2, 1]        result = [3, 1, 2]
nums = [1, 1, 5]        result = [1, 1, 5]
nums = [1, 9, 4, 6, 7]  result = [1, 7, 4, 6, 9]
nums = [3, 1, 1, 3]     result = [1, 3, 1, 3]
hints: A swap makes the array smaller exactly when a larger value moves to a later position than a smaller one it passes. The earlier the changed position, the bigger the drop, so you want the change as far right as possible.
Find the rightmost index i with nums[i] > nums[i + 1]. If there is none, the array is non-decreasing and nothing can be done.

At i, swap with the largest value to its right that is still strictly smaller than nums[i]. If that value occurs several times, use the leftmost occurrence, because then the larger value nums[i] lands as early as possible.
editorial: Lexicographic order is decided by the first position where two arrays differ, so we want to disturb the array as far to the right as possible. The disturbed (smaller) position must receive a smaller value, so it must hold a value larger than something to its right. The rightmost such position is the rightmost index i with nums[i] > nums[i + 1]; any index further right is followed only by non-decreasing values.

At i choose the replacement as large as possible but below nums[i], to keep the result as large as possible. Among equal candidates, the leftmost wins: the value nums[i] then moves to the earliest of those positions, and a larger value earlier gives a larger array.
Finding i and the partner takes one pass each: O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
